title: 3 Leadership Traits Every Teacher Needs
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who struggle with misbehavior and disrespect often lack core leadership traits -- presence, confidence, boldness, and courage -- and that these traits are not innate but the natural byproduct of three deliberate actions: deciding, committing, and delivering. Deciding means choosing an internal locus of control regardless of your roster, administrative support, or parent involvement; committing means fully embracing the SCM approach rather than mixing it with old habits; and delivering means simply following through on your stated promises day after day until consistency becomes effortless. He is explicit that his own well-known classroom management confidence isn't inborn, but the result of practicing these three actions, and he closes by reframing leadership as something you do rather than something you wait to feel.
points: Leadership traits like presence and confidence are framed as a decision plus consistent action, not a fixed personality trait.
Choosing an internal locus of control means taking responsibility for classroom outcomes regardless of roster, admin support, or parent involvement.
Full commitment to one approach, rather than blending old habits with new ones, is presented as necessary for the traits to develop naturally.
Delivering is defined simply as following through on stated promises, even when it initially requires visualizing or psyching yourself up beforehand.
quotes: They tend to have an external locus of control and difficulty grasping that they alone can create the teaching experience they want.
Locus of control, whether internal or external, isn’t so much who you are, but rather a decision you make.
Not only will SCM work as it should, but your presence, confidence, boldness, and courage will grow naturally and without effort.
With SCM—or any success method regardless of endeavor—you have to perform. There is no way around it. The good news is that anyone can do it.
I’ve been told that my classroom management confidence borders on the absurd. But it’s not inborn.
